title: The RL router beats the heuristic by 5.5 points of on-time rate — make it permanent?

scenario.role: You're the fulfillment-ops analyst at Palletworks
scenario.situation: An RL-based order-routing policy has been running against the old capacity-aware heuristic for a full quarter, randomly split per order — a quarter that included the holiday surge. Looking at the quarter's overall on-time-in-full (OTIF) rate, Miguel, the ops director, sees the RL router beating the heuristic by 5.5 points and wants to make it the permanent router.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "Over the full quarter, the RL router's on-time-in-full rate beats the heuristic by 5.5 points. It's the better router — make it permanent."
scenario.question: Did the RL router's edge hold up through the holiday surge, or was it strong during normal volume and weak (or worse) once the surge hit? Split by period before making it the permanent router.

columns.name: period
columns.description: normal or holiday_surge — normal volume versus the holiday-surge window within the quarter

columns.name: arm
columns.description: rl_router or heuristic_router — which routing policy handled this order, randomly split 50/50 within each period

columns.name: on_time_in_full
columns.description: 1 if the order was delivered on-time and in full (OTIF) — the reward

guidingQuestions: Reproduce Miguel's number: OTIF rate for arm == rl_router minus heuristic_router, pooled across the whole quarter.
Now compute the same gap separately within period == "normal" and within period == "holiday_surge". Does it look the same in both?
What share of the quarter's orders fall in the holiday_surge window versus normal? How does that affect a pooled average if the two periods tell different stories?
Why might a routing policy trained on normal-volume warehouse conditions behave differently once surge volume hits capacity constraints it rarely saw in training?
The whole point of choosing a router is how it performs during the highest-stakes period — the surge. Which number should actually drive Miguel's decision?
suggestedApproach: Reproduce the pooled gap: mean(on_time_in_full) for rl_router minus heuristic_router across all rows.
Split by period and recompute the gap within "normal" and within "holiday_surge" separately.
Check the share of orders in each period — normal volume should dominate the pooled average.

Name the mechanism: the RL policy was trained/tuned mostly on normal-volume conditions; holiday-surge volume creates capacity binds and routing tradeoffs it rarely encountered, while the heuristic's explicit capacity rules degrade more gracefully.
Recommend based on the holiday_surge gap — the regime where routing quality matters most and where the policy will actually be tested — not the pooled average.

notebook.intro: Five steps: reproduce the pooled win, split it by regime, and judge the router on the conditions that matter most.

cells.title: Reproduce the pooled gap
cells.explain: On-time-in-full rate for the RL router against the heuristic, across every order.
cells.code:
means = df.groupby("arm")["on_time_in_full"].mean() * 100
pooled_gap = means["rl_router"] - means["heuristic_router"]
print(f"pooled gap: {pooled_gap:+.2f} pts")
means.round(2)
cells.reads: Pooled, the RL router looks decisively better. The pool mixes two very different operating conditions.

cells.title: Split by regime
cells.explain: Recompute the gap inside normal volume and inside the holiday surge separately.
cells.code:
by_period = df.groupby(["period", "arm"])["on_time_in_full"].mean().unstack() * 100
by_period["gap"] = by_period["rl_router"] - by_period["heuristic_router"]
by_period.round(2)
cells.reads: The advantage is large in one regime and gone in the other. Note which regime is which.

cells.title: Check which regime dominates the pool
cells.explain: See what share of orders each period contributes to the pooled average.
cells.code:
share = df["period"].value_counts(normalize=True) * 100
print("share of orders by period (%)")
share.round(1)
cells.reads: Normal volume dominates the data, so the pooled number is mostly a statement about quiet weeks.

cells.title: Name the mechanism
cells.explain: The RL policy was tuned mostly on normal conditions. Look at how each router holds up as constraints bind.
cells.reads: Both degrade under surge, but the heuristic's explicit capacity rules degrade more gracefully than a policy that rarely met these binds in training.

cells.title: Decide on the regime that matters
cells.explain: Routing quality matters most under surge. Put the pooled number beside the surge number.
cells.code:
surge_gap = by_period.loc["holiday_surge", "gap"]
pd.DataFrame(
    {"gap (pts)": [pooled_gap, surge_gap]},
    index=["pooled across both periods", "holiday surge only"],
).round(2)
cells.reads: Making the RL router permanent on the pooled number bets on an edge that disappears exactly when the business needs it.

teachingNote.naiveRead: Pooled across the full quarter, the RL router beats the heuristic by 5.5 points of OTIF. That reads as a clear, durable improvement — obviously make it the permanent router.
teachingNote.theTrap: The quarter isn't one stable operating regime — holiday-surge volume creates warehouse capacity binds that don't show up during normal volume. Split by period and the story reverses: during normal volume, the RL router has a large genuine edge (+9.5 points). But during the holiday surge — the period where routing quality actually matters most, and precisely when the business needs reliable OTIF — the RL router is worse than the heuristic (-3.9 points). The RL policy was tuned on conditions where capacity rarely binds; once it does, the heuristic's explicit capacity-aware rules handle the tradeoffs better than a policy that never learned to operate under that constraint. Because normal-volume orders make up 70% of the quarter, the pooled average is dominated by the easier regime and hides the surge-period reversal.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Split any reward comparison by operating regime whenever conditions plausibly differ (and holiday surge is about as plausible as it gets in fulfillment), and weight the decision toward the regime that matters most — not the one that dominates the data by volume. Here, the honest surge-period gap is negative for the RL router: it underperforms the heuristic by 3.9 points exactly when reliable fulfillment matters most. Tell Miguel: don't make the RL router permanent off the pooled number. Either retrain it with real surge-volume data (or explicit capacity constraints) before trusting it in that regime, or run the heuristic during surge windows and the RL router during normal volume — a regime-aware policy, not a single pooled winner.
howToGetThere: Compute the pooled gap: mean(on_time_in_full | rl_router) minus mean(... | heuristic_router) across all rows ≈ +5.5 points.
Split by period: normal-period gap ≈ +9.5 points (RL router well ahead); holiday_surge gap ≈ -3.9 points (heuristic ahead).
Check period composition: normal volume is 70% of the quarter, so it dominates the pooled average and hides the surge-period reversal.
Name the mechanism: holiday-surge volume creates warehouse capacity binds the RL policy rarely trained on; the heuristic's explicit capacity rules degrade more gracefully under that constraint.
Recommend a regime-aware decision — use the surge-period gap for surge-window routing, not the pooled average.

numbers.label: Share of the quarter that is holiday surge

teachingNote.lesson: A policy's pooled performance over a test window only means what you think it means if the operating environment stayed constant throughout — and physical operations (warehouse capacity, seasonal volume) are exactly where it often doesn't. A policy's advantage measured under normal conditions doesn't automatically carry into a capacity-constrained surge, especially when the policy was tuned on data that rarely included that constraint. Whenever a known regime shift falls inside your test window, split the result by regime before trusting a pooled average — and weight the decision toward the regime you actually care about most, not the one with the most rows.
